statement: The cross product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ is a binary operation on two vectors in a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean vector space, computed in coordinates as $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \det \begin{bmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{bmatrix} = [\mathbf{a}]_{\times} \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \\ b_3 \end{bmatrix}$.

symbols.meaning: First vector operand with components (a_1, a_2, a_3)
Second vector operand with components (b_1, b_2, b_3)
Cross product (vector product) of vectors a and b
Skew-symmetric matrix representation of vector a
Angle between vectors a and b

properties.why: Magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors
Conversion of the cross product to multiplication by a skew-symmetric matrix
The cross product vector is orthogonal to both vectors a and b
Relation to the Gram determinant and Lagrange's identity
Vector triple product expansion formula (BAC minus CAB)
Transformation law of the cross product under a 3x3 matrix M
Application of the product rule of differential calculus to bilinear operations

assumptions.assumption: Vectors lie in a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean vector space
assumptions.breaks_when: The dimension of the vector space is not 3, or the space lacks orientation or Euclidean metric

failure_modes.mode: Inverting cross product equation a x b = c
failure_modes.cause: Vector a is not orthogonal to vector c (a . c != 0) or a = 0

failure_modes.mode: Matrix transformation identity with singular matrix
failure_modes.signature: Expression (det M)(M^-1)^T (a x b) is undefined
failure_modes.cause: Matrix M is singular (det M = 0), meaning M^-1 does not exist
